title: Lone working and your safety
respondents: Everyone who works alone for us: care staff, field care supervisors, care coordinators who visit, on-call managers and office staff who work alone
summary: An anonymous November survey, Part 1 of two linked parts with driving and travel: safe travel, risks known before visits, equipment, check-in follow-up, getting help, leaving when unsafe, abuse and harassment, and out-of-hours support. About 9 minutes.
purpose: Tests whether the lone working controls work from the worker's side: safe travel, information about risks before a first visit, safety equipment, the check-in and escalation system, getting through for help, freedom to leave, and how abuse and harassment from people we support, households and the public are reported and handled. It also carries the all-staff view of out-of-hours on-call support. It is the annual lone working survey named in the Lone Working and Staff Personal Safety Policy and the Violence and Aggression Towards Staff Policy, feeds their risk assessments, and is one of the reasonable steps to prevent third-party and sexual harassment.

timing.when: Once a year, opening on the first working day of November for 2 weeks, with the driving and travelling survey (SUR-STF-021) as Part 2; and 2 to 4 weeks after a serious safety incident, to the whole branch care team where 10 or more people
timing.trigger: A serious safety incident (optional branch send)

introduction:
This is Part 1 of {{organisation}}'s yearly survey about your safety at work; Part 2 is about driving and travelling. Please think about the last 12 months. It takes about 9 minutes, in paid working time. It is anonymous: we cannot see who answered, and our reports never show results for fewer than 5 people. To report an incident, phone the office or the On-call Manager and record it before your shift ends.

This survey cannot be used to raise a concern, because we cannot see who answered. To raise a concern, speak to any manager or our Speaking Up Lead, or use our Whistleblowing (Speaking Up) Policy.

This survey is not for urgent concerns. If you are worried about your safety or someone else's, or need help now, phone the office or, out of hours, the On-call Manager (number in your staff handbook). In an emergency, call 999.
privacyNotice:
{{organisation}} uses your answers to make lone working safer. Our legal reason is our legitimate interest in keeping our staff safe.

The survey is anonymous: we do not record your name, so your answers cannot be traced to you. CareFlow records only which branch an answer came from. Please do not write names or addresses. Only the HR Manager looks at individual answers. Our reports show results only for groups of 5 or more people, and comments and branch results for abuse and harassment only for groups of 10 or more. If a comment tells us someone may be at risk of harm, we will act on it as far as we can.

We keep individual answers for 1 year after the survey closes, under our Records Management and Retention Policy. To ask about how we use information, contact the HR Manager or our Data Protection Officer. You can also complain to the Information Commission.
closingMessage: Thank you. A reminder: if you need help but cannot talk freely, phone the office or On-call Manager and use the code phrase, or raise the CareFlow emergency alert. If you are in danger, call 999. If you cannot speak, listen to the questions and cough or tap the phone to answer; on a mobile, press 55 when asked, so the call is put through to the police.

sections.title: Abuse and harassment
sections.introduction: These questions are about people we support, anyone in their home, or members of the public, not colleagues. You do not have to answer the questions about what happened to you, and our employee assistance programme can help if they bring back difficult feelings (number in your staff handbook).

howToRun: The HR Manager runs it with the Registered Manager. Use Send or schedule with everyone in your branches, repeating yearly from the first working day of November, kept open 14 days, and schedule the driving and travelling survey (SUR-STF-021) for the same moment as Part 2, telling staff in one message. Skip November's pulse. CareFlow records the branch of each anonymous answer, never the person.

After a serious safety incident, send a one-off copy 2 to 4 weeks later to the whole branch care team, only where that is 10 or more people; never to the small group around the person harmed, who get the debrief and supervision the Violence and Aggression Towards Staff Policy sets. Never in September, and fold it into the November run when within 4 weeks. CareFlow refuses an anonymous survey that would reach fewer than 5 people.

It is done in paid working time. Paper on request, in a sealed envelope to the HR Manager, who enters it alone with Record response, recorded as anonymous. Set one reminder after 1 week in Reminders and follow-up: on an anonymous survey CareFlow sends it to everyone who has not answered, with no personal link, and never to one person.

Who may open individual answers: the HR Manager only, who reads comments each working day while the survey is open. This is set in Who can see the answers: individual responses are limited to the HR Manager, and results to the HR Manager and the Registered Manager, showing from 5 answers. Super Admin, Admin and the person who made the survey can always see both, so keep those roles to staff who may open them. On-call Managers and Care Coordinators, whose support is being rated, never open them or see results below organisation or branch level.
actingOnResults: Comments are read each working day while the survey is open. A current risk at an identifiable home goes to the Registered Manager the same working day, so the Field Care Supervisor reviews that person's behaviour and aggression risk assessment (within 7 days after an incident, and before the next visit where it involved physical violence, a weapon, sexual harassment or threats to harm), under the Violence and Aggression Towards Staff Policy. Risk to a person we support goes to the safeguarding lead the same working day. Wrongdoing is a speaking-up concern with the Nominated Individual as case owner; harassment by a colleague is logged by the Nominated Individual as an anonymous report. Nobody tries to identify the writer.

How to count: positive means Very good or Good, Strongly agree or Agree, Always or Usually, or Yes, I am sure, leaving out Does not apply to me, Don't know and Prefer not to say. For needing help but not phoning on-call, No is the good answer. Never show a result for fewer than 5; flag 5 to 9; show branch results and comments only for 10 or more; report the abuse and harassment questions at organisation level unless 10 or more in a branch answered them.

Library triggers: reporting "No" or "Yes, some of it" from 20% or more of those affected means an under-reporting action in the violence and aggression risk assessment and team briefings; any sexual harassment option chosen goes to the sexual harassment risk assessment, and identity-based remarks to the harassment risk assessment under the Equality, Diversity and Inclusion Policy, at aggregate level only; late check-in follow-up or getting through below 90% positive means the Deputy Manager checks escalation timescales and on-call answer times (missed calls returned within 15 minutes); not being sure what to do when you cannot talk, or when to phone 999, NHS 111 or on-call, above 10% means refreshers at team meetings and spot checks; anyone needing help but not phoning on-call is explored at team meetings and in the on-call review.

All results go into the general lone working risk assessment review (every 12 months) under the Lone Working and Staff Personal Safety Policy and the violence and aggression general risk assessment, with actions in the service improvement plan, reviewed at the Health and Safety Meeting. Keep individual answers for 1 year after the survey closes under the Records Management and Retention Policy.

regulatoryBasis.source: Health and Safety Executive, Lone working: employers must manage the risks to lone workers, including violence, and keep in touch with them
Health and Safety Executive, INDG73 Protecting lone workers: how to manage the risks of working alone (assess the risks, train, supervise, keep in touch, and review with the workers)
Independent Office for Police Conduct, Silent Solution: making a 999 call from a mobile when you cannot speak (press 55 when prompted)
Equality Act 2010, section 40A: an employer must take all reasonable steps to prevent sexual harassment of employees, including by third parties
Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014, Regulation 17(2)(e): seek and act on feedback from staff
